input: A single-stage compressor raises nitrogen from 1 bar to 4 bar, with an inlet temperature of 313 K. For isentropic compression with a heat-capacity ratio of 1.4, the discharge temperature works out at 465 K. Isentropic compression is the idealised case: the gas is compressed with no heat transfer to the surroundings and no irreversibility inside the machine, so the discharge temperature it gives is effectively the lowest that the pressure rise can produce. The estimate is set by the pressure ratio and the heat-capacity ratio alone; it contains nothing about the machine beyond the gas it handles. It is important to note that the isentropic estimate excludes mechanical losses. Friction in the bearings and seals, irreversibility in the valves and the flow passages, and heat picked up from hot machine parts all add to the discharge temperature, and the installed machine's measured discharge temperature is higher than the estimate for exactly that reason. The gap between the measured figure and the estimate is thus a property of the machine, rather than an error in the relation, and the gap will tend to widen as the machine wears. Used the other way round, the estimate also bounds what can be claimed for the machine: no real compression of this gas between these pressures discharges colder than the isentropic figure. The estimate therefore serves as the reference against which the machine is judged; a measured discharge temperature close to it indicates a machine in good order, while a growing gap indicates losses that maintenance can recover.
